name: Hyperbolic discounting
statement: People discount the near future more steeply than the far future, so a reward available now can outweigh a larger one later that they would have chosen when both were distant.
meaning: Exponential discounting applies the same rate to every interval, so a choice made today between two future dates survives the wait. Hyperbolic discounting applies a rate that falls as the horizon lengthens, so the ranking flips once the sooner reward comes into reach. Someone may prefer $110 in 31 days to $100 in 30 days and still take $100 now over $110 tomorrow. Economic work commonly summarises that pattern with a simplified version, the quasi-hyperbolic or beta-delta form, in which one parameter discounts everything except the present and ordinary exponential discounting handles the rest. Beta below 1 is present bias and beta of 1 is dynamic consistency. That parameter, rather than the shape of any curve, is what the experiments test.

origin.note: "Specious reward: A behavioral theory of impulsiveness and impulse control" reviewed the literature on impulsiveness and argued that hyperbolic curves describe how the effectiveness of a reward falls with delay. Frederick, Loewenstein and O'Donoghue record the function Ainslie proposed as D(t) = 1/t. The year before, Ainslie had reported in the Journal of the Experimental Analysis of Behavior on pigeons given a small immediate food reinforcement for pecking a key and a larger delayed one for not pecking it. Most subjects pecked the key on more than 95% of trials. Three of 10 learned to peck a differently coloured key earlier on, which removed the tempting option. Laibson's 1997 Quarterly Journal of Economics paper, 'Golden Eggs and Hyperbolic Discounting', carried the idea into economics through a consumer whose only commitment device is an illiquid asset.

evidence: The classic demonstration is an implied discount rate that falls as the horizon lengthens. Thaler asked respondents what sum in one month, one year or ten years would leave them indifferent to $15 now. Frederick, Loewenstein and O'Donoghue give the median answers as $20, $50 and $100, implying annual rates of 345%, 120% and 19%. Those are median answers from one sample under one matching procedure, and Thaler's paper could not be opened during this check, so the figures are attributed to that review rather than read off the original. The same review reports that fitted hyperbolic functions beat exponential ones on such data. The testable core is the preference reversal, and the review cites four human studies and two pigeon studies for it. A footnote records that all of them are synchronic: the subject holds both preferences at one sitting. The diachronic version, in which subjects brought back 30 days later have switched, follows from the synchronic one only if discounting is stationary. Laibson used the beta-delta form to explain why consumption tracks income, why consumers have asset-specific marginal propensities to consume, and why financial innovation might lower welfare by supplying too much liquidity.

replication.headline: Present bias is small or absent when the reward is dated money and clear when the reward is work: a meta-analysis of 217 estimates puts beta near 0.97 for money and 0.88 for effort.
replication.detail: Andreoni and Sprenger gave 97 subjects a convex time budget, splitting an allocation between a sooner and a later date across 45 decisions, and equalised the transaction costs and the delivery risk of the two payments. They estimated beta at 1.004, standard error 0.002, alongside an annual discount rate of 0.300. The rejection of beta = 1 was marginal and pointed towards future bias. Augenblick, Niederle and Sprenger then ran the same allocation over real work, seven weeks of Greek transcription and Tetris. Money gave beta = 0.974, standard error 0.009, and effort gave 0.888, standard error 0.033, with the two rejected as equal, chi-squared(1) = 6.37, p = .01. A between-subjects repeat on 200 further students gave 0.997 for money and 0.892 for effort. Offered a commitment device at a price of zero, 47 of 80 subjects took it, raising from 0.1 to 0.9 the chance that their earlier allocation counted. Present bias over effort predicted that choice, though the raw correlation was 0.225 and explained about 5% of the variance. Augenblick and Rabin had 100 participants choose task loads over seven weeks and found they wanted 10 to 12 percent fewer tasks in the present than at any future date, beta = 0.83. Imai, Rutter and Camerer collected 220 estimates from 28 articles using the convex time budget, then averaged 217 of them after dropping three influential observations. The random-effects average is 0.9663, standard error 0.0147, p = .0297 against beta = 1, and the multi-level average is 0.9518. Monetary studies give 0.9723 and 0.9758, neither distinguishable from 1. Effort studies give 0.8815 and 0.8802, p = .0001 and p = .0004. Money is not settled either. Balakrishnan, Haushofer and Jakiela paid 494 participants in Kenya through M-Pesa and found beta between 0.902 and 0.924, but only where the same-day payment landed immediately after the session rather than at the close of business. Ruggeri and colleagues tested the reversal at scale, putting five intertemporal choice anomalies to 13,629 people in 61 countries on a preregistered plan. The choices were hypothetical and each anomaly had one item. Rates for the four main anomalies ran from 13.8% for absolute magnitude to 40.1% for gain-loss asymmetry, 54% of participants showed at least one, and every anomaly appeared in every country.

study.cite: Imai, T., Rutter, T. A., & Camerer, C. F. (2021). Meta-analysis of present-bias estimation using convex time budgets. The Economic Journal, 131(636), 1788-1814.

limits: The one multi-site preregistered study located is Ruggeri and colleagues, and its choices were hypothetical. Searches of Crossref, Europe PMC, Semantic Scholar and the journals themselves found no incentivised multi-site replication of the beta-delta estimates on the Many Labs or Registered Replication Report pattern. Four lines of work put the falling discount rate down to the elicitation rather than to time preference. Read, Frederick, Orsel and Rahman found that discount rates drop with horizon when a delay is described as an interval and stay flat when the same delay is given as a calendar date, an interaction of F(3,165) = 9.4, p < .0001. Halevy separated stationarity, time consistency and time invariance, and reports that about half of his time-inconsistent subjects had stationary preferences, which present bias alone cannot produce. Chakraborty, Calford, Fenig and Halevy re-analysed the Andreoni and Sprenger data and found 43 violations of the weak axiom of revealed preference among the 36 subjects who chose only corners, 34 of them towards less impatience under the convex time budget than under a choice list. Enke, Graeber and Oprea paid subjects to value a sum 'shrunk 12 times' by 4% each time, a task with no delay in it, and the hyperbolic pattern appeared anyway. A beta-delta model fitted to those atemporal choices returns 0.85, standard error 0.01, where the design forces the true value to 1. Behaviour on the two tasks correlates at 0.34. Their reading is that present bias identified from the shape of the discount function is inflated, while front-end delay designs, which push both payments back by a common lag, are not confounded. Heterogeneity in the meta-analysis is close to total: I-squared is 98.08 across all estimates and 98.13 among monetary studies, so the pooled figure describes a spread rather than a value. Imai and colleagues find funnel-plot asymmetry in the effort studies, p = .0016, running towards over-reporting of present bias, and their corrections move the effort average anywhere from 0.90 to 0.99 depending on the method used. The underlying measurement has never converged. Frederick, Loewenstein and O'Donoghue plotted every study they could locate that reported a discount rate or let one be computed, and give implied annual rates from -6% to infinity. They add that the range of estimates is not shrinking over time. Cohen, Ericson, Laibson and White argue that money-earlier-or-later choices cannot isolate time preference, because a subject's financial flows on a date are only weakly linked to consumption on that date, and they report that measures of time preference explain less than 5% of the cross-sectional variation in economic behaviours involving intertemporal trade-offs.
misreadings: Hyperbolic discounting is a model, so the question a replication can answer is narrower than the name: does the present carry extra weight. Nearly every estimate above comes from the quasi-hyperbolic beta-delta form, which is not a hyperbola. It marks down the future in one step and then discounts exponentially. The second error is reading a null result over money as a null result for present bias. Andreoni and Sprenger make the point themselves: the models of temptation and self-control are about consumption, and a subject with access to modest liquidity should not be expected to show present bias over dated cash, which can be arbitraged. Imai and colleagues find that studies run where more people hold credit cards or can draw on liquid savings report less present bias. The third error is treating a null in one payment protocol as the last word. The Kenyan results turn on whether 'today' means today or within the hour. The fourth is enrolling the Global Preference Survey as a measurement of present bias. Falk and colleagues surveyed 80,000 people in 76 countries and report patience, which is the level of discounting rather than the way it changes with horizon. A fifth is the calibrated beta of around 0.7 that circulates from macroeconomic work; Andreoni and Sprenger cite Laibson, Repetto and Tobacman for that figure and set their own 1.004 against it.
